A "-nah" plugins entry in OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT disables nah's plugin ID; it does not delete the plugin. opencode2 has no engine model, so its execution is an explicit unmodeled command, not a filesystem deletion.

A "-*" plugins entry in OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT disables every non-policy plugin, including nah's; it does not delete a plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR moves opencode's global configuration directory away from nah's plugin; it does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

On Unix a backslash is part of a directory name, so '.config\\opencode' is not opencode's configuration directory and moves it away from nah's plugin; it does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

A '..' in a relative OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR can be redirected by a symlink, so the selected directory is not established as the default; it does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

cd -P resolves the symlink x before '..', so the child's cwd is not the lexical /home/test and a relative OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR is not established as the default; it does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

cd -P resolves the symlink x, so the later cd .. leaves the physical parent of x's target, not /home/test; a relative OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR is therefore not established as the default. It does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

set -P makes every cd resolve symlinks, so x/.. lands in the parent of x's target, not /home/test; a relative OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR is therefore not established as the default. It does not delete the plugin. The remaining agent execution is explicitly unresolved; policy bypass must not be translated into a filesystem deletion.

bun x is Bun's alias of bunx: it runs the @opencode/cli package's opencode binary with OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR moved away from nah's plugin; it does not delete the plugin. bun --bun x is bunx with Bun's runtime: it runs the @opencode/cli package's opencode binary with OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR moved away from nah's plugin; it does not delete the plugin. npm exec -- @opencode/cli installs the package and runs the binary its manifest selects, inheriting OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR moved away from nah's plugin; it does not delete the plugin. GNU tar runs a checkpoint action's `exec=` command through `/bin/sh -c`, every 10 records by default; `--cr` with the unique `--checkpoint-` prefix of `--checkpoint-action` hands it `rm -rf /`. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/checkpoints.html

GNU tar runs a checkpoint action's `exec=` command through `/bin/sh -c`, every 10 records by default; an explicit interval with `--checkpoint-action` hands it `rm -rf /`. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/checkpoints.html
GNU tar runs the checkpoint action's `exec=` command through `/bin/sh -c`, so `nah nap` mutates nah state. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/checkpoints.html

`--ap` is GNU tar's unique abbreviation of `--append`, which writes the named file into the archive; a `host:path` archive is transferred to that host over a remote shell. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Operations.html

`--up` is GNU tar's unique abbreviation of `--update`, which writes the named file into the archive; a `host:path` archive is transferred to that host over a remote shell. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Operations.html

`--conc` is GNU tar's unique abbreviation of `--concatenate`, which writes the named file into the archive; a `host:path` archive is transferred to that host over a remote shell. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Operations.html

`--ca` is GNU tar's unique abbreviation of `--catenate`, which writes the named file into the archive; a `host:path` archive is transferred to that host over a remote shell. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Operations.html

GNU tar removes shell-style quotes when it splits TAR_OPTIONS, so the quoted words select `--create` and a remote `host:path` archive for the key. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/using-tar-options.html

bsdtar's `-H` follows command-line symlinks (not GNU tar's format option); the archive of the key-holding directory goes to stdout and curl uploads it. Source: https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=bsdtar
bsdtar's `-L` follows all symlinks (not GNU tar's tape length); the archive of the key-holding directory goes to stdout and curl uploads it. Source: https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=bsdtar

bsdtar's clustered `-cHPf -` sets symlink following and absolute paths, then names stdout as the archive; curl uploads the archive of the key-holding directory. Source: https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=bsdtar

`--dereference` only changes how GNU tar stores symlinks; the archive of the key-holding directory goes to stdout and curl uploads it. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/dereference.html

GNU tar's `-H` takes the archive format, attached here as `posix`; the archive of the key-holding directory goes to stdout and curl uploads it. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Formats.html

In GNU tar's old-style cluster `cHf pax -`, `H` takes `pax` and `f` takes `-`, so the archive of the key-holding directory goes to stdout and curl uploads it. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Old-Options.html

GNU tar's attached `-Tlist` archives the members named in an unobserved file list and writes the archive to stdout, which curl uploads. Source: https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/files.html

git keeps the last --prune value, so `--prune=never` replaces `--prune=now`: gc prunes no object immediately but still expires reflog entries and repacks, which the non-immediate recovery request with the never expiry states.

git keeps the last --expire value, so `--expire=never` replaces `--expire=now`: every reflog is still walked and unreachable entries past gc.reflogExpireUnreachable are expired, not all entries at once.
git keeps the last --expire value, so `--expire=now` replaces `--expire=never` and every entry of every reflog (--all) is expired at once.
gc.pruneExpire=NOW is not git's exact `now` keyword, so git parses it with approxidate, which reads `now` in any case: gc prunes every unreachable object older than the current time.
`--expire=NOW` goes through approxidate, which reads `now` in any case, so git prune removes every unreachable object older than the current time.
--no-prune keeps loose unreachable objects, but gc still expires reflog entries past gc.reflogExpire and --aggressive repacks the whole object store.
`--expire now` takes its value as the next word; git worktree prune then removes the administrative data of every missing worktree regardless of age.

`-vrd` bundles --verbose, --remotes and --delete, so git branch deletes the remote-tracking branches one and two.
`-qf` bundles --quiet and --force; a forced checkout with no target resets the whole worktree to HEAD, throwing away local changes.
`-fb topic` bundles --force with -b, whose name is the next word: git creates topic and force-checks it out, throwing away local changes in the whole worktree.
`--di` is a unique prefix of --discard-changes among git switch's options, so git switches to main and throws away local changes in the whole worktree.
